utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Good afternoon to everyone. Madam Registrar, would you please call the case.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Your Honours. This is the case IT-03-69-T, the Prosecutor versus Jovica Stanisic and Franko Simatovic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Madam Registrar. The Chamber was informed, Mr. Jordash, that you'd like to raise a matter.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Yes, I would like to, please. It's concerning Mr. Stanisic's health, and it's a request to the Trial Chamber to intervene to this extent. We would request an urgent report from Dr. de Man on top of the report we've requested in relation to the Bronovo hospital and the specialist treatment Mr. Stanisic is hoping to receive at that hospital. I won't detain the Court for long, but this is our concern. First of all, as Your Honours know, Mr. Stanisic has been waiting for treatment at the Bronovo hospital for some time. As Your Honours also know, he did receive some new treatment and then that treatment was stopped because of concerns that it was not going to assist Mr. Stanisic and, in fact, might have some unpleasant side effects. Your Honours will recall we requested a report last week dealing with the developments on that issue, and, in particular, what the latest advice is and what the latest expectation is in relation to his treatment. Mr. Stanisic was told that he would receive the new treatment - this is, I think, the third type of biological treatment - and he was told that he would receive that last week. That still hasn't happened. So we are concerned about that, and we would renew our request for a report dealing with this subject as soon as possible. Our principal concern, though, at this moment is the treatment that Mr. Stanisic receives within the UNDU for his psychiatric illness. Trying to obtain information from the Registry is difficult, to say the least. But we have requested, and I won't go over the history of the requests, but, in short, on the fourth request, the Registry disclosed to us that Mr. Stanisic did, in fact, have notes relating to his treatment or his medical examinations for his psychiatric condition. Why it took four times to receive that information is still a mystery. As is, what precisely the treatment he receives is still a mystery. We requested, upon receipt of the information that there are, in fact, notes in existence, the notes. And that was two weeks ago, and we're still waiting for those notes. Apparently those notes are in a compilation of notes with other detainees' notes and it appears that it takes two weeks to redact that information before considering disclosing that to Mr. Stanisic's representatives. Again, why it would take that long to disclose medical notes to an accused is, again, still a mystery. But, putting aside the mystery, we are deeply concerned. What we've had disclosed to us is a summary purporting to be a summary of Dr. Petrovic's examinations of the accused over the last few years. It's a two-page summary, so we don't expect that this contains the kind of detail we hope the notes contains. But what it does contain is the following sentence: "The examinee constantly receives an appropriate medicament therapy aimed at lowering down the psychological disturbances but the psycho therapy is insufficient but it is -- because it is possible every seventh week when the psychotherapist is present." Now that contradicts what we've been told by the Registry, which said that Mr. Stanisic received therapy every four to six weeks. But putting that aside, what is clear, even from the scant information that the Registry provides, is that Mr. Stanisic's treatment for a serious psychiatric condition, an ongoing enduring psychiatric condition, is inadequate within the UNDU. Now, has that led to a situation where we are in a position where we're saying Mr. Stanisic is not fit? No. Has that led to a situation where his health may well be less than it should be if he had received appropriate treatment? Then that looks very likely. And that, of course, has an impact not on just Mr. Stanisic's health, which is the principle concern of Mr. Stanisic, but our principal concern is that that leads him to a position where he is not as healthy as he could be to defend this trial. And so it does engage Your Honours, we would submit, at this stage before we get to the crisis point where we are actually saying: He is not fit to continue. So to summarise and not to detain the Court any longer, we have two possible ways to proceed. One, is to go to -- through the bureaucratic obstacles which appear to be placed in front of us by the Registry. We get the notes from Dr. Petrovic in the next few days. We then engage with the Registry about the treatment. We eventually get a report from Dr. Petrovic dealing with some further questions about Mr. Stanisic's treatment and eventually perhaps the Registry will provide proper treatment within the UNDU. I can see that lasting several months, several months at a critical time in Mr. Stanisic's trial. Instead, what I would hope is that Your Honours would expedite this protracted process and ask Dr. de Man to deal with this issue, comment as swiftly as possible on whether -- what his view is of Mr. Stanisic's treatment for his psychiatric condition within the UNDU. And upon receipt of that report, we can move from there perhaps more swiftly and obtain, as quickly as possible, proper treatment for Mr. Stanisic within the UNDU so that he can focus on his trial rather than worrying about his treatment. And we've tried to, as much as we can - I speak on behalf of the Stanisic Defence and also the accused - keep Mr. Stanisic's health out of the picture as much as we can. And that's involved a huge amount of work behind the scenes, making sure that Mr. Stanisic maintains a proper grip on what is going on. But there comes a point when the Registry put so many obstacles in front of us, the treatment looks inadequate, Mr. Stanisic constantly struggles with his health, and, despite to wanting to keep moving forward, clearly, to us, appears like he's struggling to the point of danger. And there comes a point, in our submission, when we have to start thinking about applying to suspend the trial. Because we are representing a client who is extremely ill, on the one hand, the notes appear to indicate that his treatment is inadequate in the UNDU, and every time we go to the Registry all we receive are obstacles. The latest obstacle being, Oh, it has got nothing to do with us. It is to do with the commander of the UNDU. So this is the situation we're in. I'm sorry to take the time up with the Court, but I wanted the Court to understand our deep frustration and concern about Mr. Stanisic and hope that the Court will react to that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Jordash. I think it is not a secret that the Chamber always wants to pay appropriate attention to these kind of problems. It is also not a secret that there's a thin line between concerns about treatment and the impact of treatment on the trial. We'll consider what you just said, and you're primarily asking for an additional report by Dr. de Man dealing with adequacy of the treatment and -- and his assessment of the present situation of Mr. Stanisic, that's what you're asking for.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Your Honour, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We'll consider it. And any other matter?

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: No, thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: No other matter. Then could the witness be brought into the courtroom, which gives me time, at least, to deal with one issue. Yesterday the first eight pages of 1D05008 were exhibited but not yet, at that time, uploaded. I do understand that now the first eight pages of the B/C/S and the corresponding English pages are uploaded as 1D05008.2. A number had already been reserved for it; that was D695. And I think that there were no objections, Ms. Friedman, which means that 1D05008.2 is admitted into evidence as D695.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Good afternoon --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Mr. Gagic. I'd like to remind that you that you're still bound by the solemn declaration you've given at the beginning of your testimony, and Ms. Friedman will now continue her examination. Ms. Friedman, please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MS. FRIEDMAN
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MS. FRIEDMAN
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Mr. Gagic. You've testified that you were employed continuously in the Serbian MUP and that the only pension you receive is from the Serbian MUP; correct?

utterances.speaker: GVOZDEN GAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. FRIEDMAN
utterances.text: And it's based on your uninterrupted service from 1980 to 2006?

utterances.speaker: GVOZDEN GAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. FRIEDMAN
utterances.text: Could we now have 65 ter 6377. Oh, and can we go into private session, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We move into private session.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: We're in open session, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Madam Registrar.

utterances.speaker: MS. FRIEDMAN
utterances.text: Did -- from what you said, did they share information freely about the units that they commanded?

utterances.speaker: GVOZDEN GAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, they didn't have independent units under their command. Badza was the overall commander for the TO Staff; whereas Arkan was the commander of one of the units under that staff. In other words, Badza was Arkan's superior.

utterances.speaker: MS. FRIEDMAN
utterances.text: Does that mean that Arkan reported on his activities to Badza?

utterances.speaker: GVOZDEN GAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. On the activities for which he was charged by the Staff, he would submit reports on a regular basis.

utterances.speaker: MS. FRIEDMAN
utterances.text: Do you know specifically which activities he was charged by the Staff? I -- I take it you mean the TO Staff?

utterances.speaker: GVOZDEN GAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I mean the TO Staff. Well, he was primarily charged with the reception and training of volunteers and their deployment to the neuralgic points where was the greatest risk from the Croatian forces in the area of Slavonia. He was also charged with providing supplies for his units. He took part in the operations carried out around Vukovar.

utterances.speaker: MS. FRIEDMAN
utterances.text: You also observed Goran Hadzic at the centre. Did Hadzic also receive information from -- let's start with Arkan?

utterances.speaker: GVOZDEN GAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I had never seen Goran Hadzic in any formal capacity, say, in a meeting, or at a gathering. I saw him come in and go out of the centre on a number of occasions.

utterances.speaker: MS. FRIEDMAN
utterances.text: Did you have an opportunity to observe his relationship with Arkan when he was at the centre?

utterances.speaker: GVOZDEN GAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. Nor did I take any particular interest in it.

utterances.speaker: MS. FRIEDMAN
utterances.text: Did you observe his interaction with Badza?

utterances.speaker: GVOZDEN GAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I would follow that because their meetings would take place in the same location where my unit was billeted, i.e., the Saponia offices in Erdut. They had meetings regularly every morning, and I would attend some of them, though most of them I did not.

utterances.speaker: MS. FRIEDMAN
utterances.text: On the ones that you attended, would Badza brief Hadzic on the activities of the Territorial Defence?

utterances.speaker: GVOZDEN GAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: We misunderstand each other. I meant the Badza and Arkan meetings. I did not attend any meetings where Hadzic would be present.

utterances.speaker: MS. FRIEDMAN
utterances.text: So you did not -- is it your evidence, then, that did you not observe Hadzic and Badza interacting?

utterances.speaker: GVOZDEN GAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is my evidence, that I did not.

utterances.speaker: MS. FRIEDMAN
utterances.text: Yesterday you were asked whether the SAO Krajina was looking to the Ministry of Defence to assist them with a training -- with training combatants by establishing a training centre in Prigrevica. And you answered, at T.17190: "By that time, the idea had ripened and requests were sent, and the top police and military leadership decided - I don't know exactly when - that the training centre should be set up in Erdut rather than Prigrevica, which lacked the necessary infrastructure for such training grounds." This is the training centre in Erdut that was run by Arkan; correct?

utterances.speaker: GVOZDEN GAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. FRIEDMAN
utterances.text: When you say that the police and military leadership decided to set it up, are you referring to the Serbian Ministry of Defence and Serbian MUP?

utterances.speaker: GVOZDEN GAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I meant the Serbian Ministry of Defence and the Serbian MUP. Because Prigrevica sits in the territory of the Republic of Serbia, whereas Erdut is in the SAO Slavonia and Baranja, or, rather, Croatia. Therefore, the RSK Ministry of Defence was not able to decide to set up a training centre in the territory of Serbia. Such a decision could have been taken only by the Serbian Ministry of Defence, and it was for that reason that the decision was made to open up a centre in Erdut.

utterances.speaker: MS. FRIEDMAN
utterances.text: So that centre in Erdut was opened up by the Serbian MUP and Ministry of Defence?

utterances.speaker: GVOZDEN GAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The centre in Erdut was opened by the Ministry of Defence and the Ministry of police of the Republic of the Serbian Krajina, because it was not possible to set up a centre outside of Slavonia in order to train individuals residing in Slavonia.

utterances.speaker: MS. FRIEDMAN
utterances.text: And you were asked whether General Ivanovic provided Arkan with military registration plates as a means of getting through border crossings, and you stated: "I don't know how true it is because the relationship between Arkan and the people from the MUP was much closer." That's at T.17198. Is that a reference to the Serbian Krajina MUP and the Serbian MUP?

utterances.speaker: GVOZDEN GAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, the Serbian MUP, too, because through Badza, who was an employee of the Serbian MUP and the commander of the special anti-terrorist unit, I in fact meant the Serbian MUP. Because I had never seen any other vehicle in possession of the Arkan's unit with military registration plates and that's why I said that I found it unusual.

utterances.speaker: MS. FRIEDMAN
utterances.text: You testified last week that you "had known Arkan from before on several different bases." On what bases did you know him?

utterances.speaker: GVOZDEN GAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Arkan is several years my senior. As a youth, I had an opportunity to learn of Arkan, not to meet him in person, because he was a bouncer working in a number of discotheques. So many wanted to become acquainted with him. So this is still the period before I started working for the MUP. It was from that period that I was aware of his nickname, Arkan. From the later period, I knew that he was involved in criminal activities abroad and that he been convicted for these crimes. And to tell you frankly, I was surprised to see him leading a select number of Serbian patriots later.

utterances.speaker: MS. FRIEDMAN
utterances.text: Did you -- you say you were surprised. Did you ask anyone in a position of authority why Arkan was the one training volunteers?

utterances.speaker: GVOZDEN GAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: There was no one to ask, really. It was a fait accompli even before I could show any sort of interest in that and exhibit any sort of influence. He had, by then, become such a prominent personality in Slavonia that it became superfluous to raise an issue like that.

utterances.speaker: MS. FRIEDMAN
utterances.text: You testified about his relationship with the Novi Sad Corps that: "Arkan's relations with the Novi Sad Corps Command and lower-ranking officers of that corps was professional. It was quite decent. He conducted himself as a subordinate. He did not in any way stick out from the system for the conduct of combat that was in force in the armed forces." Did you know that in his conduct within battles he was also committing crimes?

utterances.speaker: GVOZDEN GAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, save for excessive use of force in combat, if that can be treated as crime, I am not aware of specific cases where Arkan or members of his guard committed crimes in person. It is possible, however, that in an exchange of fire excessive force was used.

utterances.speaker: MS. FRIEDMAN
utterances.text: Did you believe that the excessive force was the intention of the Novi Sad Corps Command?

utterances.speaker: GVOZDEN GAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I'm not sure that that was the intention, but it was definitely there. For instance, in one of the actions aimed at neutralising two snipers, a silo was destroyed through excessive use of force. After all, they were only targeting two individuals, and probably there was no other way of neutralising them, since they - although there were only two of them - did have under firm control an area of some 2 kilometres.

utterances.speaker: MS. FRIEDMAN
utterances.text: I'd now like to call up Exhibit P1219.

utterances.speaker: MS. FRIEDMAN
utterances.text: This is a transcript from an interview given by General Biorcevic, and he described co-ordinated actions involving Arkan's Men. And I'd like to, in particular, take you to the -- the last thing that he says, which is: "We surround a village, they enter it, kill those who refuse to surrender and we go on." I take it you were not aware that this role was endorsed by General Biorcevic?

utterances.speaker: GVOZDEN GAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I don't see anything that is an issue here. It is stated here: "... those who refuse to surrender." Well, I suppose they would be combatants firing upon Biorcevic and his men, and if they refused to surrender, of course, that they would neutralise them, kill them.

utterances.speaker: MS. FRIEDMAN
utterances.text: Okay. If that's how you take it. I would like to move on, then, to --

utterances.speaker: MS. FRIEDMAN
utterances.text: I'm finished with this exhibit.

utterances.speaker: MS. FRIEDMAN
utterances.text: -- during your time in Dalj, if you were aware that Arkan and his men were committing crimes against civilians, ethnic Croats and Hungarians?

utterances.speaker: GVOZDEN GAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MS. FRIEDMAN
utterances.text: Sir, Dalj is a small village; correct?

utterances.speaker: GVOZDEN GAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. FRIEDMAN
utterances.text: And, on the night of October 4th, you were in Dalj?

utterances.speaker: GVOZDEN GAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. FRIEDMAN
utterances.text: You also -- you testified, in fact, that you and your men were patrolling -- you and the other men in your unit were patrolling Dalj while you were there.

utterances.speaker: GVOZDEN GAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. FRIEDMAN
utterances.text: So are you saying that you are not aware that 26 prisoners were killed by Arkan and his men on that night of October 4th?

utterances.speaker: GVOZDEN GAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm not aware of it.

utterances.speaker: MS. FRIEDMAN
utterances.text: We've heard evidence that there was a public rally afterwards because the bodies were washing up on the Danube and that the villagers gathered, and Arkan took responsibility for these crimes. It was a quite a big rally, and the local police were there to guard it. Are you saying that you were not aware of that either?

utterances.speaker: GVOZDEN GAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: My unit was not present there, nor were we engaged to enforce law and order at that rally. Had it been a larger rally, on a more massive scale, perhaps I would have been aware of it. But I suppose it was just the local villagers who gathered there, and I never came to learn of that meeting.

utterances.speaker: MS. FRIEDMAN
utterances.text: Could we have P11, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could I ask you one question. I'm trying to analyse your last answer. You said it was a -- "had it been a larger rally, on a more massive scale, perhaps I would have been aware of it." Now, at the same time, you say, I'm not aware of it, and you're saying, Would it have been larger, then perhaps I would have been aware of it. Which suggests that you have knowledge that it was a small-sized rally. Was it?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No. Had the rally been larger, our unit, too, would probably have been engaged to maintain law and order there. Since it had not been engaged, I assumed that it must have been a smaller gathering. Besides, based on what the Prosecutor said, based on her interpretation, this happened several days after our arrival in Dalj, at which point we were still dealing with certain arrangements, billeting, making the premises we were allocated to habitable, and so on.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You said several days. What made you believe -- when Ms. Friedman said there was a public rally afterwards, what makes you believe that it was several days?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, Ms. Friedman said that the event took place on the 4th of October.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And she said we've heard evidence that there was a public rally afterwards. You say it was several days after your arrival, at which point you were still dealing with certain arrangements. So I tried to understand your evidence in detail. On the one hand, you say, Well, must have been a small one because we were not called to keep -- to keep order; at the same time, you say, We were not actually yet operational because we are dealing with other matters. Now, that -- these are two different explanations. Could it have been that it was a larger rally but that you were still busy with your accommodation, et cetera, or is that impossible?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I cannot claim either that it was small or large. My conclusion was that it was a small rally, a sort of spontaneous gathering of citizens which could not have lasted more than it -- well, it didn't last for five or six hours. It was probably ended quite soon thereafter. And when I was describing the time-frame, that was based on the date that I was given, the 4th of October. And I assumed that the citizens gathered soon after the incident, and it all happened in that period of time shortly following our arrival and deployment there.

utterances.speaker: MS. FRIEDMAN
utterances.text: We'll now turn to P11. This is a police report that documents --

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Sorry to -- I'm just wondering if it might be fair to the witness to put the details of the rally to him and see if that assists. It's just a suggestion.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Of course, I'm not opposing to that, Ms. Friedman. At the same time, the witness says, We were not involved in any way in a rally which took place briefly after the 4th of October. What is then -- should we say, Do you even not remember that was it a sunny day or that there were a thousand people, or that there were 50 people, or would that change anything.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Well, to be honest, I can't remember the size of -- what the evidence is in relation to this subject. I can't remember the size of the rally. So I think that -- my first thought was that we would all be assisted with a reminder as to the size of the rally, and the witness then may have interesting observations to make about the size of the rally and it may --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: He is not aware of the rally. How could he possibly say anything about the size of the rally?

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Well, if it's a rally with 20 people, he might say, I was dealing with a situation where there was -- with 50 refugees somewhere, so a rally of 20 people would not have come to my attention.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Well, I would not object if you would seek further evidence to clarify what this witness could tell us or could not tell us about the rally, but I also think that there's no obligation to do so. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MS. FRIEDMAN
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours. I believe he has had sufficient information, including that it was a response to the bodies washing up from the river, and that most of the village gathered, and that the police were securing it. I think that is sufficient, but I can review over the break.

utterances.speaker: MS. FRIEDMAN
utterances.text: Now, could you please look at this police report, Mr. Gagic, a -- I would like you to read it, and please let me know when you've finished.

utterances.speaker: MS. FRIEDMAN
utterances.text: Could I also ask that it be lifted so that we see the signatories on the bottom. And we can already go to the second page in English.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I've read it.

utterances.speaker: MS. FRIEDMAN
utterances.text: At the bottom, the document is signed by the Dalj police station commander, Zeljko Cizmic. Did you meet Mr. Cizmic when you were in Dalj?

utterances.speaker: GVOZDEN GAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MS. FRIEDMAN
utterances.text: And on the left-hand corner we see who it was sent to. The first addressee is police administration secretary of the Autonomous District of Slavonia, Baranja, and Western Srem. Do you know who that was at the time?

utterances.speaker: GVOZDEN GAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, we are using different titles here. I think that the secretary, who would in today's terms be a minister, was still Bogunovic. Though not Veljko Bogunovic who was the commander of the unit but a different Bogunovic who was in charge of the MUP. The heading of the document indicates that -- we can perhaps look at the top of the document, and there you will see the Republic of Croatia, Ministry of the Interior, Police Administration, Osijek, Baranja. Based on what we can read there, there had still not been a more serious transformation in that particular SUP, which was a bit outlying.

utterances.speaker: MS. FRIEDMAN
utterances.text: Yes. And the last addressee that we see on this is Special Unit Commander Zavisic. And that is Zavisic that reported directly to Badza; correct?

utterances.speaker: GVOZDEN GAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Zavisic was one of Badza's assistants.

utterances.speaker: MS. FRIEDMAN
utterances.text: And you testified that when you arrived, it was for the purpose -- "the crime prevention police had not been established." But -- isn't this exactly what the police Commander Cizmic was trying to do, to get accountability and prevent future crimes?

utterances.speaker: GVOZDEN GAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, it clearly follows from this that he did advocate that position.

utterances.speaker: MS. FRIEDMAN
utterances.text: I'd like to now move into private session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We move into private session.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: We're in open session, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Madam Registrar.

utterances.speaker: MS. FRIEDMAN
utterances.text: You received information in relation to the crimes in Zvornik from the ICTY Office of the Prosecutor; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: GVOZDEN GAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The War Crimes Prosecutor received it from the International Tribunal, and I got it from the War Crimes Prosecutor through the Republic of Serbia.

utterances.speaker: MS. FRIEDMAN
utterances.text: And you participated in meetings with OTP investigators and attorneys about the cases, handing over the files; is that right?

utterances.speaker: GVOZDEN GAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MS. FRIEDMAN
utterances.text: And the Zvornik case included both Yellow Wasps paramilitaries and others, such as Branko Popovic; correct?

utterances.speaker: GVOZDEN GAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. FRIEDMAN
utterances.text: Branko Popovic, also known as Marko Pavlovic, he was the head of the Territorial -- he was the commander of the Territorial Defence unit in Zvornik; is that right?

utterances.speaker: GVOZDEN GAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. FRIEDMAN
utterances.text: And when asked about this man you stated: "I am not aware of any links he would have with either the MUP or the DB of the Republic of Serbia, nor was such a link established during investigation." Did you interview any of the witnesses who testified against Branko Popovic?

utterances.speaker: GVOZDEN GAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MS. FRIEDMAN
utterances.text: Were you aware of the evidence that they gave before the investigative judge?

utterances.speaker: GVOZDEN GAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I read the book by Natasa Kandic -- I'm sorry, the book related to the Skorpions. As far as the Yellow Wasps are concerned, I was not actively involved in the case.

utterances.speaker: MS. FRIEDMAN
utterances.text: So, in that case, on what basis did you say that your investigation didn't lead to any connections between Mr. Popovic and the Serbian MUP?

utterances.speaker: GVOZDEN GAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Based on talking to him.

utterances.speaker: MS. FRIEDMAN
utterances.text: To Mr. Branko Popovic?

utterances.speaker: GVOZDEN GAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. FRIEDMAN
utterances.text: Just to make sure, I believe I've asked you, but you are not familiar with the file in relation to the case? Your only familiarity is from talking to him?

utterances.speaker: GVOZDEN GAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as his connections with the MUP, all I know is from talking to him. I know the rest of the story from the documentation you made available to the prosecutor.

utterances.speaker: MS. FRIEDMAN
utterances.text: And that documentation that we made available, it did link Mr. Popovic to the Serbian MUP; isn't that correct?

utterances.speaker: GVOZDEN GAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I had no occasion to see that part of the documentation. I only saw photographs of persons linked to this crime, their personal details that were rather imprecise and, in fact, inaccurate.

utterances.speaker: MS. FRIEDMAN
utterances.text: "Persons linked to the crime." Do you mean -- is that victims or perpetrators?

utterances.speaker: GVOZDEN GAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Perpetrators.

utterances.speaker: MS. FRIEDMAN
utterances.text: How did you know that their details were imprecise if you weren't involved in investigating?

utterances.speaker: GVOZDEN GAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: From the moment when I received the prosecutor's request, including their photographs and their personal details, I proceeded to identify these persons, to locate their places of residence, and prepare the action to arrest them. And, in this process, I found a lot of mistakes, errors in the documentation provided by the prosecutor concerning their personal information.

utterances.speaker: MS. FRIEDMAN
utterances.text: So such as date of birth, address, contact detail, that sort of thing?

utterances.speaker: GVOZDEN GAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I mean their years of birth were inaccurate. In two cases, photographs were swapped, including names and surnames. And in one case, the address was wrong.

utterances.speaker: MS. FRIEDMAN
utterances.text: Okay. With respect to the Skorpions, you testified that you received documentation based on which you were to arrest the alleged perpetrators and that you studied that documentation and established that they had no connection with the Serbian MUP or DB. Did you find this documentation -- did you find in this documentation that the Skorpions were reporting to Vaso Mijovic?

utterances.speaker: GVOZDEN GAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I learned that from that book I mentioned by Natasa Kandic which includes the transcript of the trial of the Skorpions. But before reading the book, I didn't know about the connection between Vaso Mijovic and this group.

utterances.speaker: MS. FRIEDMAN
utterances.text: And did you know that Vaso Mijovic worked for the Serbian DB?

utterances.speaker: GVOZDEN GAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I know that Vaso Mijovic worked for the DB of Serbia and the DB of Montenegro.

utterances.speaker: MS. FRIEDMAN
utterances.text: So then there was a connection between the Serbian DB and the Skorpion trial --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Jordash.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: May I address you in the absence of the witness, please. I do think that there is to be greater precision in the way that these issues are put because I think there's been some misrepresentation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Let's first establish -- Witness, do you understand the English language?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, no.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Not a word? Apart from yes or no, perhaps, but ...

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Nothing. Apart from yes, nothing.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could you take off your earphones for a second, please. Mr. Jordash.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: My learned friend asked the witness whether he had found in this documentation that the Skorpions were reporting to Vaso Mijovic. But I think that the more accurate statement is that one witness out of the trial stated that the Serbian MUP were reporting to -- sorry, the Skorpions were reporting to Vaso Mijovic. And that's significant because none of the suspects said that they had any connection to Vaso Mijovic. Kovac said that the Skorpions reported to Vaso Mijovic. But Kovac was also the gentleman who claimed not to have heard of Commander Medic, and we all know Commander Medic's connection to the Skorpions. So to put it to the witness as if this documentation is riddled with suggestions that Vaso Mijovic was connected to the Skorpions is quite misrepresentative of the situation. It is Natasa Kandic who is absolutely convinced the Skorpions were connected to Vaso Mijovic and one particular individual --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Jordash, I'm going to interrupt you already here. The problem of the Chamber is we do not know what documentation has been made available at the time, so if you say it misrepresents what was sent, we couldn't give you an answer because we do not know what was sent and what was the content of it. Ms. Friedman, please also keep this in mind if you respond to Mr. Jordash, the best way of dealing with the matter would be to be very precise in stating what that documentation contains as information so as to avoid that Mr. Jordash jumps up and puts a question before the Chamber the Chamber cannot rule upon. Well, of course, we could try to find the procedural means by saying, Please tell us exactly what you did give, or try to agree on that, or we could hear further evidence on that. But, of course, that is not the most efficient way of proceeding. So, therefore, if Mr. Jordash says this, and this, and this is to be found in this documentation, let's just assume that Mr. Jordash knows exactly what has been provided. Do you know that, Mr. Jordash?

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Well, I know what has been provided to us from the Prosecution in relation to the Skorpions trial and I'm presuming Ms. Friedman is working from that documentation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Okay. That is an assumption. So we do not know yet. I interrupted you. I'd like, if you would not mind, first give Ms. Friedman already an opportunity to see whether she knows how to resolve this problem for the Chamber.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: From our perspective, I think that the Chamber is either going to, in our submission, have to see this documentation or the Prosecution are going to have to agree certain things, such as no witness other than Kovac linked Vaso Mijovic to the Skorpions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Let's hear whether Ms. Friedman has a good solution for us.

utterances.speaker: MS. FRIEDMAN
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honours. First, I would like to note that I was not finished this line of questioning, that I followed up on what the witness said about Natasa Kandic. Second, the documentation that I am referring can be easily ascertained. It is -- which I was getting to. It is not witness evidence. I was not going to go into the witness evidence. But the Skorpions judgement itself - which Mr. Jordash is familiar with and which is uploaded as 1D -- or let me see, 1D1321 - does refer to the documentation that was provided by the ICTY. So what I was going ask this witness is if he received the same documentation and I was going to ask him about those particular documents, not witness evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Jordash, there seems to be an indirect reliance on the materials sent by the ICTY, such that Ms. Friedman relies on what was said in the judgement about what was received from the ICTY.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Sorry, I'm not sure I'm following this. If it -- the Skorpion judgement certainly did not find that Vaso Mijovic was in charge of the Skorpions, that's what -- but perhaps I'm missing the point. But that's what -- the judgement did not find Kovac to be honest on that issue.

utterances.speaker: MS. FRIEDMAN
utterances.text: I am not seeking recourse to the judgment or the witness evidence. The question is -- the way to ascertain the documents that were provided to Mr. Gagic and to his ministry is by looking to the actual written record of what was provided and that's contained in the Skorpions judgement. And from the description of the documents in the Skorpions judgement, we can identify that two of them were also admitted in this trial. So I was just going to direct his attention to the evidence that is before this Trial Chamber and that was handed over to his office and to the investigative judge of the Skorpions trial.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Now, let's get back to what triggered the whole discussion, which was about Mijovic, but I have to go back to -- One second, please. Yes, I think the appropriate question to be put to the witness would be: What he -- he said that Mijovic worked for the DB. We could ask him what he learned from the documentation, in terms of reports given to Mijovic. And if he says, I did not learn anything from this documentation, we can ask whether he learned that from the book from Kandic and whether he verified -- or whether he ever found it in the documentation sent. And then, of course, we could also ask him whether he had gone through the whole of the documentation or whether he had seen only part of it. And then we can deal with it without the suggestions where apparently Mr. Jordash has some problems with. Let's try to resolve the matter at this moment in this way. I leave it in your hands at this moment, Ms. Friedman. Could you put on your earphones again. From the time it takes, I feel guilty about speaking too quickly. There should be someone who stops me as well. Please carefully listen to the next questions that Ms. Friedman will put to you, Mr. Gagic.

utterances.speaker: MS. FRIEDMAN
utterances.text: Mr. Gagic, I'd like to focus now on your investigation and not anything you read afterwards. So your investigation of the Skorpions, did that include reading documentation in a file provided by the ICTY?

utterances.speaker: GVOZDEN GAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MS. FRIEDMAN
utterances.text: So you did not actually investigate this case, looking for a link to the Serbian MUP, did you?

utterances.speaker: GVOZDEN GAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct. I did not look for a link, nor was it part of my investigation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could we then perhaps, Ms. Friedman, go back to one of the previous answers. Ms. Friedman put to you as one of your answers being: "I am not aware of any links he," and then we are talking about Popovic, "he would have with either the MUP or the DB of the Republic of Serbia, nor was such a link established during investigation." Now, yes, Mr. Bakrac.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: May I said that it's the different case.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, I know that. But -- I know it's a different case. But I wanted to know from you, does that mean, if you are referring to an investigation, that you had not read any of the documentary materials which was sent by the ICTY?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Correct. All the information was in the possession of the prosecutor. I received only a videotape from which I was supposed to identify the persons appearing on the film, to locate them, and to organise the operation to arrest them. All the rest was in the hands of the prosecutor.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: So whatever links there may have been with Popovic, Mijovic -- you knew apparently that Mijovic was linked to the DB. That's what you said. But apart from that, you had no information available which was sent by the ICTY. You only focussed on who do I have to arrest, and that's it?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Correct. But I know Mijovic personally. He is still alive.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Everything you know comes from the book of Natasa Kandic rather than from documentation sent by the ICTY.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Ms. Friedman.

utterances.speaker: MS. FRIEDMAN
utterances.text: In that case, I would just note, as I think it will be helpful, that it's on page 13 of the English and 15 of the B/C/S of the Skorpions judgement, which is 1D1321, where they refer to the list of documentation, and two of the documents on the list are P1084 and P1453. If the witness hasn't reviewed that documentation in his investigation, I don't think it is relevant to call it up. But for the Chamber it would be relevant.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: No. Well, unless you had doubts as far as his answers are concerned. If you want to put it more directly to him. From what I understand from the witness is that he only used any material which he needed to identify -- to identify the persons he had to arrest.

utterances.speaker: MS. FRIEDMAN
utterances.text: And that he was not seeking to make a connection with the Serbian MUP.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. That is -- I would say that is implicit in what I just said.

utterances.speaker: MS. FRIEDMAN
utterances.text: I have another question about the deployment. You said that you became familiar with the Trnovo operation. Were you aware that one of the units deployed was the Plavi unit?

utterances.speaker: GVOZDEN GAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was aware of it but only later.

utterances.speaker: MS. FRIEDMAN
utterances.text: And that the Plavi unit was commanded by Ljubomir Milojevic. And this is the same man who was in Dalj, as the deputy commander. Is that right? Can you confirm that?

utterances.speaker: GVOZDEN GAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm not aware of these facts.

utterances.speaker: MS. FRIEDMAN
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Gagic, for answering my questions. I have no further questions at this time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Ms. Friedman. Mr. Jordash, any further questions before Mr. Bakrac has an opportunity to --

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Only a handful, if I may.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: A handful, yes, yes. It's difficult to look at the clock, what a handful exactly means, but five fingers is five minutes?

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: I think that's --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: That's sufficient, I think. Thank you. Further Cross-examination by Mr. Jordash:

utterances.speaker: MS. FRIEDMAN
utterances.text: Yesterday you were asked about Dusan Momcilovic, and towards the end of the day this was, and you were asked the question: "So my question to you" --

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: And this is Your Honours, page 17263.

utterances.speaker: MS. FRIEDMAN
utterances.text: "So my question to you is whether this willingness to join in on the struggle and offer any assistance also reflects the attitude of the police stations in Eastern Slavonia in 1991 and 1992?" And you answered: "Yes, the police force of Eastern Slavonia, as well as the police force in Knin was ready and prepared to provide assistance to all the organs who needed it. Now, what their abilities were is a different matter, but whatever they had at their disposal, they were prepared to place -- to -- to use, to help other organs that needed it in Krajina and Republika Srpska." That rather generalised discussion, I want to try to be a bit -- understand what you meant with specifics. Were you talking about police, professional police responsibilities, or were you talking about combat, or -- or what were you talking about?

utterances.speaker: GVOZDEN GAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, the question was put to me after I viewed a video-clip of the speech. And I was asked what this meant. And I said that it meant that the RSK police forces were prepared to provide every possible assistance to all other organs within Krajina and, if possible, to provide assistance in activities from the sphere of the police in Serbia as well.

utterances.speaker: MS. FRIEDMAN
utterances.text: That's right. Because Momcilovic was talking about, when he descended into specifics, he was talking about crime-scene examinations, forensic analysis, things which seemed to be limited to police activities. Is that what you were talking about as well?

utterances.speaker: GVOZDEN GAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. FRIEDMAN
utterances.text: Thank you. Thank you, Mr. Witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: And thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Bakrac.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour. With your leave, I will take no more than ten to 15 minutes. I will follow-up on the topic raised by my learned friend, Mr. Jordash.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Gagic, Ms. Friedman showed you documents yesterday where Momcilovic described his membership as of a certain date. Previously in the course of your examination, you were able to see that Momcilovic had been issued with an official ID of the MUP of the Republic of Serbia, signed by Nikola Curcic in 1992, and you explained why this was. First tell us: Were official IDs of public security and state security of the Republic of Serbia different at all?

utterances.speaker: GVOZDEN GAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The IDs that were introduced for public and state security were not different at all, until the point when badges were introduced, and these differed even where it came to within public security branch itself.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: You say "official badges were introduced." When was this?

utterances.speaker: GVOZDEN GAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I cannot state with any certainty when it was, but I believe it was in 1994 or 1995. Actually, right after the legislation governing the engagement of the Ministry of the Interior was amended. At that point, the IDs that had been used up to that point were withdrawn, and new IDs and badges were introduced.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: Is my understanding of what you said correct: You are now speaking of public security, are you not? Because, in fact, in state security, these changes were effected later on.

utterances.speaker: GVOZDEN GAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, as I said, the official IDs of public and state security were completely identical until the format of these IDs was changed. Once the old IDs were withdrawn and new IDs were introduced, these official badges differed even within public security because those who were charged with combat against organised crime had different sort of badges from those who were involved in just crime prevention or even from those that differed -- that were involved in traffic policing.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Can Mr. Bakrac please repeat his question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Bakrac, could you re-start your question.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, I apologise to Their Honours.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreter notes that we also missed the last sentence of what the witness said.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, but could we -- even part of what the witness said was missing. Witness, I'll take you back to your last answer. I read a portion and then you're invited to add but only add what you then said. You said: "Once the old IDs were withdrawn and new IDs were introduced, these official badges differed even within public security because those who were charged with combat against organised crime had different sort of those" -- no. Yes. "... a different sort of badges from those who were involved in just crime prevention or even from those that ..." And could you please repeat what you then said.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Those who were involved in traffic infractions. And I am not aware at all what the case was in state security.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. So you say they were exactly the same up till the moment that the old IDs were withdrawn, and the new ones, even within the public security, would not be identical but could differ, depending on whether it was badges for those who were to combat organised crime, those who were involved in crime prevention, or even traffic police. Now, one of the questions which was not answered yet, was the time where the old badges were withdrawn in state security and public security the same, or was it at different times?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'm not aware of that. I don't know.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You don't know. Please proceed, Mr. Bakrac.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: Well, let's state what it is that you know for sure. And that is that up until 1994 or 1995, both public and state security had identical IDs; is that right?

utterances.speaker: GVOZDEN GAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. The witness told us that he didn't know whether it was different at other times. But let's proceed, Mr. Bakrac.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: Mr. Gagic, if my understanding of what you said is correct, you had quite a few friends and acquaintances who were thrown out of the Croatian MUP. Persons who worked in the MUP of the Republika Srpska -- or, rather, the Republic of the Serbian Krajina, starting from the autumn of 1991 until August of 1995, when Storm happened, these persons, were they entitled to benefits arising from years of service they had had at the time they worked in the Croatian MUP still when they were working for the RSK MUP?

utterances.speaker: GVOZDEN GAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I know that there weren't many such cases, but one person who belonged to my unit, after the war ended and once Slavonia was reintegrated into Croatia, stayed on and continued working in the Croatian MUP, and that was in the town of -- if I should name it, it's the town of Ilok.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: My question had to do with the police. Well, let's take it this way. Does the -- did the Republic of Croatia recognise the existence of the RSK; if you know?

utterances.speaker: GVOZDEN GAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, it did not.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: The persons who have not returned to the Republic of Croatia yet, are they able to use the benefits arising from the time that they worked for the RSK MUP, would they be able to use it in Croatia now?

utterances.speaker: GVOZDEN GAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: You say that you had many acquaintances. Are you familiar of a case where such people would be reporting that -- those years of service in the Republic of Serbia in order to have those years of service with the RSK counted into -- counted toward their benefits in Serbia?

utterances.speaker: GVOZDEN GAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. A great many people did start working for the MUP of the Republic of Serbia whilst staying for these four years in the territory of the RSK and working there. When they withdrew from the RSK territory, they continued working for the Serbian MUP because that was where -- where they had their employment and those years of service were counted toward their current employment. Were credited to them.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: Do you know of cases where individuals who, later on, post-Storm in 1995, were admitted to the Serbian MUP and after having been admitted, that they sought that their previous years of service within the RSK be recognised?

utterances.speaker: GVOZDEN GAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I can't give you specific cases, but I'm sure that based on the documentation that they would have, that those years of service would be credited to them.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: Is it fair to conclude that individuals who were admitted to the MUP of the Republic of Serbia at a later date stated in their applications for employment also the years of service during the period when they worked for the RSK MUP?

utterances.speaker: GVOZDEN GAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Ms. Friedman.

utterances.speaker: MS. FRIEDMAN
utterances.text: These last few questions have been leading.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, they were. Witness, could you tell us, you say that you're sure that, based on the documentation, that the years of service in the RSK MUP would count. What makes you sure about that? Is there a legal basis for that, is there -- what is it that you believe this? Because we're less interested in what someone believes but rather in what someone knows.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Those members of the RSK police who, in the period between 1991 and 1995 started working in the Republic of Serbia whilst remaining in the territory of the RSK, have had their years of service recognised. Those who started working for the MUP of the Republic of Serbia after 1995, if they had valid documentation, they, too, would have had the years of service recognised which they spent working for the RSK MUP. I know that from some of the personal contacts I had.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Tell me what those personal contacts were.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] A group of policemen whom I met later in 2000 or 2001. I can't give you their names, though I might recall one or two, if you give me enough time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I give you all the time you need for it.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I think that one of these cases was a man called Radisevic. He entered into employment -- entered into employment there after 1995. Then a man called Loncarevic, who also began working there after 1995.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Was their period of working of the RSK taken into account in -- in respect of -- of benefits or pensions?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, yes. When I say that they had their years of service recognised, that implies that their pensionable years of service were recognised. These years were regarded as though they had been spent within the service of the Serbian MUP.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: So if you earlier told us that you didn't know of any individual cases, that it's not true, because you're now reporting two individual cases where that happened.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I don't know. I'm afraid that there must have a misunderstanding. When I said that I didn't know of individual cases, I meant persons who would have their years of service recognised, whilst they were in the MUP of the Republic of Croatia.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I'll re-read the question, and I'll re-read your answer. Mr. Bakrac, you may proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Sorry to interrupt. May I request again an earlier break.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. It depends a bit on -- could we just consider if -- if Mr. Bakrac also has only five questions, one handful, then we might -- of course, we'll stop if there's a need to do that. But if we could finish -- Ms. Friedman, how much time would you still need?

utterances.speaker: MS. FRIEDMAN
utterances.text: Maybe just one or two more questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: One or two questions. Another solution would be -- I'm thinking, of course, first of all, about Mr. Stanisic. I'm also thinking about the witness, if we could conclude his testimony before a break. But I leave it, if you say, no, Mr. Stanisic would not -- prefer to take a break already himself and he would want to hear the last questions and answers, then we'll take the break now. Otherwise, I would suggest perhaps that Mr. Stanisic considers whether he wants -- whether he insists to be present for those last few questions and answers.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: I'll take instructions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. And let Mr. Stanisic feel perfectly free to decide. I mean, his right to attend the proceedings is, of course, fully respected.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Well, I know he is feeling extremely ill today and wasn't --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: No, that's -- that's not my problem. My problem is whether -- whether he insists on having -- this last five minutes of testimony, to attend that, yes or no. Of course, I have to keep in mind also the interests of the witness. But, of course, the fundamental right of Mr. Stanisic is above that.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: If Mr. Stanisic could have a break but the proceedings can continue.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And then, Mr. Bakrac, how much time would you still need?

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Some 15 minutes, Your Honour. Ten to 15 minutes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Then we'll -- then we'll take the break now. We'll take a break, and we'll resume at 25 minutes past 5.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Bakrac, isn't it true that you earlier indicated that you'd need ten minutes? Because time used should be deduced, not added to the time you earlier indicated. But I'll check that.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I'm sorry, but certain things cropped up that I have to clarify, and that's why I'm asking for additional time. The answers of the witness produced something that I want to clear up.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Try to -- I mean, ten minutes initially, and now, after quite some minutes, another 15 is not what we expect you to do. So please proceed as efficiently as possible. Which does not mean speak very quickly, but efficiently examine the witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour. Could we please call up D456, that is MFI'd, and I need page 43 in B/C/S and page 41 in English.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: The document is under seal, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. We need to go into private session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We move into private session.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: We're in open session, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Madam Registrar.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: And then you went on to say that these laws -- you agreed that the laws and regulations were adopted after the Operation Storm. Okay. So that -- those are your answers in relation to that. Do you know why the regulations were adopted so late in the day, 1995, some distance after the critical period of the war in Croatia?

utterances.speaker: GVOZDEN GAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, after the first wave of Serb policemen leaving the ranks of the Croatian MUP and joining the RSK MUP, well, they did not go to the Serbian MUP directly but went to other towns within the RSK to find employment in the RSK MUP. Likewise, after Flash and Storm, when they were chased away from the territory of the RSK, yet again they were in a position where they were jobless and applied to the Serbian MUP, which admitted those people.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: So if I understand you correctly, this was not the result of an agreement that had been reached in 1991 or 1992. It was the result of the events of Operation Flash and an agreement formed at that point between those who had been in the RSK MUP and those who were wanting now to join the Serbian MUP. Am I right?

utterances.speaker: GVOZDEN GAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes. They were bylaws that were adopted after 1995; whereas an interstate -- or inter-governmental treaty was stipulated between Croatia and Serbia only at a much later date. That's to say, 1998 or 1999.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: So, in summary, if I can put it this way, this is a situation which is quite different, for example, from the situation where VJ officers were sent to the Republika Srpska and there was an agreement at the time that they would receive their pensions and benefits. This is a totally different situation to that, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: GVOZDEN GAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Their employment was not interrupted. They were JNA officers, and, as such, were dispatched both to the Republika Srpska and the Republic of Serbian Krajina, where they joined the VRS and SVK respectively. This had already been regulated in a federal Law on All People's Defence. Now the police did not have such a possibility to resort to.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: Thank you. Thank you, Mr. Witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Bakrac.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I didn't want to interrupt my learned friend Mr. Jordash and intervene. At page 58, line 23, the date is wrong. Perhaps I should just ask the witness when it was that the inter-governmental treaty between Croatia and Serbia was signed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We could ask the witness. Could you tell us when the inter-governmental treaty between Croatia and Serbia was signed.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It was signed sometime in 2008. And it did not apply to the police force only, but to all the employees.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you. Ms. Friedman, do you have any further questions.

utterances.speaker: MS. FRIEDMAN
utterances.text: No further questions, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I would have one. Questioned by the Court:

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Witness, you told us that Arkan was reporting to Badza, being his subordinate. Was -- were those reports in writing or oral?

utterances.speaker: GVOZDEN GAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mostly oral. And mostly these were meetings held at 9.00 every morning.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You said: "Mostly oral." Are you aware of any written reports by Arkan to Badza?

utterances.speaker: GVOZDEN GAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I didn't see a single written report.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Now, you said that he reported on the activities for which he was charged by the Staff, the TO Staff. Are you aware of Arkan engaging in any activity outside the assignments that were given to him by the TO Staff?

utterances.speaker: GVOZDEN GAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Arkan carried out certain activities directly on the orders from the Novi Sad Corps. I don't know what these activities specifically were, but I do know that he had been engaged by the corps command. He had been charged by certain tasks that had not gone through the Staff command.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Now, would he also engage in activities for which he did not receive any assignment at all? That is, neither from the TO, nor from the Novi Sad Corps.

utterances.speaker: GVOZDEN GAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That I don't know. Except for obtaining supplies or contacting journalists, there were certain things that he carried out independently. He probably was engaged in certain activities without having received direct orders for them.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And those certain things, apart from obtaining supplies or contacting journalists, could you shed any further light on what those certain activities were?

utterances.speaker: GVOZDEN GAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Specifically he conducted training in a way that was pretty much autonomous. And I mean the training of his volunteers, once the instructors were trained for that job. He would go out into the field, regardless of whether there was an order from the corps command or the TO Staff command. But I did not mean combat activities. When it came to combat activities, whatever he did was under the command of the TO Staff or the Novi Sad Corps command.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Now this Chamber has heard evidence about persons being killed by Arkan's Men. Would that be an activity he engaged in without any instructions; or can you tell us anything about that? Because you said the way in which he conducted training, obtaining supplies, contacting journalists. Now this is a totally different category. Could you tell us anything - and if you can't, please tell us as well - whether such activities, of which the Chamber received evidence, would be on the basis of an assignment or would be an activity he engaged in all by himself?

utterances.speaker: GVOZDEN GAGIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm not able to answer the question, other than by drawing an inference.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I would like you not to draw any inferences. I'd rather ask about your knowledge about facts. I have no further questions. No further questions? Then, Mr. Gagic, this concludes your testimony in this court. I'd like to thank you for coming to The Hague and for having answered the questions that were put to you by the parties and by the Bench, and I wish you a safe return home again.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. I have a question for you. Will my military ID that was given to the Registry be given back to me now or at a later date?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: The parties had an opportunity to look into that document. None of the parties have used that opportunity. Is there any need to have it or to have it in evidence? If not, it will be returned immediately to the witness.

utterances.speaker: MS. FRIEDMAN
utterances.text: No need here. We have the scans --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I do not hear from Mr. Jordash. I also do not hear from Mr. Bakrac, but he is in another conversation. Mr. Bakrac, any need to further inspect the booklet?

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Then it will be returned to the witness and it will not be part of the record. You'll receive it back, Mr. Gagic. You may follow the usher and leave the courtroom.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Jordash, are you ready to call your next witness?

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Yes, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Then -- oh, I should have instructed the usher to bring the next witness in. Madam Registrar, is there any way to speed up -- that the usher, without delay, brings the witness in?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I'm afraid that we have to be patient.

utterances.speaker: MS. FRIEDMAN
utterances.text: Your Honours --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. FRIEDMAN
utterances.text: -- just a brief procedural matter in relation to the last witness. There was a video I showed at the end of yesterday, 65 ter 6228, and I didn't formally tender it. The transcript was covered more than the video so we're just getting a fuller version of the video and would want have it admitted then. But perhaps it could receive an MFI number.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. That we already reserve at least a number for the video. Any objection against that video? Ms. Friedman, could you give the further details. Madam Registrar, Ms. Friedman would like to tender a video but it is not uploaded yet in the precise format -- the precise format in which --

utterances.speaker: MS. FRIEDMAN
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated]

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: So if we reserve a number for that video.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour, it will be MFI'd.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Jordash, no protective measures?

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: No, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Mr. Selak. Before you give evidence, the Rules of Procedure and Evidence require that you make a solemn declaration, that you will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth. The text is now handed out to you. May I invite you to make that solemn declaration.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Selak. Please be seated.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Jordash, are you ready to --

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Your Honour, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I must admit, we're all aware of the rulings of the Chamber what would be the starting point. And finding a large number of pages of exhibits to be used from other cases surprised me a bit, but, of course, I do not know how you intend to use them.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Well, I -- I -- I think Your Honours will not need to be concerned.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: That's good to hear. That's good to hear. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Mr. Selak. Could you, for the record, please, give your name and date of birth, please.

utterances.speaker: OSMAN SELAK
utterances.text: Osman Selak; 20 May 1935.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: First of all, I want to deal with some formalities, in terms of your previous testimony at this court. You - is this correct? - testified in the Milosevic trial on the 12th and 13th of June, 2003?

utterances.speaker: OSMAN SELAK
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: And have you had an opportunity to review that testimony before coming to court today?

utterances.speaker: OSMAN SELAK
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: And have you had an opportunity to make any clarifications or amendments that you wish to make to that testimony and have none to make?

utterances.speaker: OSMAN SELAK
utterances.text: No. I stand by my testimony in the Milosevic case fully, and there is nothing to change there.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: And what you said during that case was in accordance with the truth?

utterances.speaker: OSMAN SELAK
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: And you'd answer the same if asked the same questions today?

utterances.speaker: OSMAN SELAK
utterances.text: Yes. I hope that I haven't forgotten, since it is human for persons to forget or for their memories to fade over the years. But I do stand fully by what I stated in the Milosevic case.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Selak.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: May I tendered this previous testimony uploaded as 1D03920 and 1D03921 and the associated exhibits which have been notified to the Registry.

utterances.speaker: MS. HARBOUR
utterances.text: No objection, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: No objection from the Prosecution. Ms. Harbour -- and we talking about the 12th and the 13th of June, 2003, isn't it.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Your Honour, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Associated exhibits, also no problems.

utterances.speaker: MS. HARBOUR
utterances.text: None, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Then --

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Can --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Still numbers have to be assigned to those because we have the numbers now of the -- that were assigned in the Milosevic case.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Could I also indicate something else which needs to be taken in account. The war diary, which is 1D05178, from our 19 -- our 92 bis filing is already exhibited in this trial as P1282. And similarly, 1D05184 is already tendered in this trial as P1307. That exhibit is missing the cover page. We have asked the Prosecution to add the cover page to that exhibit which carries ERN 00184109.

utterances.speaker: MS. HARBOUR
utterances.text: Your Honour, since that's already an admitted exhibit, I'm not sure if the Prosecution should add it or if --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. What needs to be done is that, if a document is incomplete, to replace the originally admitted document by a completed one, or to add one page, then it, first of all, should be -- that page should be uploaded, and then Madam Registrar will ask permission from this Bench to replace the original exhibit by the new one. And since it is not a complete different one, the only matter we have to keep in mind is that the numbering of the pages in e-court might change, which may cause problems at a later stage when reading the transcript. But, first of all, the cover page should be uploaded and then Madam Registrar will seek the Chamber's decision on replacing the original one. Or adding something to the original one. Apart from that, anything else, Mr. Jordash?

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: No. Not in relation to that issue. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Which means that you say two out of ...

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: 31 exhibits have already been admitted.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: If I look at the list, I have a list of 29. Yes, 31 in its totality. Madam Registrar, could at least 29 numbers be reserved for associated exhibits. And, of course, first of all, we have to assign a number to the -- to the Milosevic transcript which was tendered as well.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. First Milosevic transcript 1D03920 will receive number D699. And 1D03921 will receive number D700. And associated exhibits will receive numbers within the range from D701 up to, and including, D729, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Madam Registrar. D699 and D700 are admitted into evidence. For the others, we have to finalise that, but the numbers are reserved.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. May we have 1D05439 on the screen. I don't think this goes against Your Honours' orders. I hope not. It's a chart --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Depends what you are doing with it. Let's have a look.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: What you're going to see in front of you in a moment, Mr. Selak, is a chart with documents listed on the left side and comments on the right-hand side. This is 1D05439. When you arrived in The Hague, were you provided with this chart and a list of -- sorry, a number of documents and asked to provide your comments in the right-hand side of this chart?

utterances.speaker: OSMAN SELAK
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: And were the comments you made -- let me go back a bit. Did you review the comments you made for any amendments or clarifications that you wanted to make?

utterances.speaker: OSMAN SELAK
utterances.text: The only thing I see in this chart is the title of the document and not the comments I made. For instance, for 3722 or P02524, I can see the title of the document, but not the comment given.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Can we -- let's see if we can remedy that.
